pages.hook: In the USA, fruit is sold in two ways: each, like one mango, or by the pound, like bananas. Learn both before you shop.

mythfact.s: In the USA, many fruits are sold by the pound.
mythfact.why: A pound (lb) is about 450 grams. Bananas and apples often cost “a dollar a pound”.

mythfact.s: American stores always sell fruit by the kilo.
mythfact.why: The USA mostly uses pounds and ounces, not kilos.

mythfact.s: In Miami, you can hear both English and Spanish at the market.
mythfact.why: Many people in Miami speak Spanish, and many speak both languages.

mythfact.s: The small sticker on a banana is only for decoration.
mythfact.why: The sticker has a number code that helps the cashier find the price.

decode.q: How many bananas does the list ask for?
decode.why: “2 lb bananas” means two pounds of bananas.

compare.br: In Brazil, many people buy fruit by the kilo, or by the unit, and often ask for the price at the street market (feira).
compare.us: In the USA, you see “each” or “per pound” on the sign. A pound is a bit less than half a kilo.
compare.tip: If the sign says “lb”, the price is for one pound, not for the whole bag.
compare.ask: What fruit do you buy every week? Say: “I’ll take two pounds of…”

quiz.q: The sign says “$2 each”. You want four. You pay…

quiz.why: lb = pound, a weight of about 450 grams.

quiz.q: The seller says “Anything else?” You are finished. You say…
quiz.why: That’s all, thanks closes the order.

pages.polite: Say **please** when you ask and **thank you** when you pay. “I’ll take…” is a normal way to choose.

pages.title: Reading quest — Fruit day in Miami
text: Today I went to a fruit stand in **Miami**. The sun was hot and the fruit looked great. A man smiled and said, “Good morning! Can I help you?”
I asked, “**How much are** the mangoes?” He said, “**They’re two dollars each**.” I said, “**I’ll take four**, please.” Four mangoes cost eight dollars. That was a **good deal**!

Then I asked, “**Do you have** bananas?” “**Sure!**” he said. “**They’re one dollar a pound**.” I wanted **two pounds**. A pound is a little less than half a kilo, so I was not sure about the size. But the bananas were nice.
The man put the fruit on the **scale**. “**That’s ten dollars**,” he said. Eight dollars for the mangoes and two for the bananas. I gave him a ten-dollar bill and said, “Here you go. Thank you!”

On the way home, I remembered an old English rhyme: “Oranges and lemons, say the bells.” At a market in London, a seller says, “**A pound of oranges, please.**” Fruit stands are a little like a small song.
Tonight I will eat a mango. It is sweet, and it makes me happy. Tomorrow I want to buy tomatoes and an onion!
